row: | | Huang et al., *Advancing Transformer Architecture in Long-Context LLMs: A Comprehensive Survey* (2023 ⚑): sorts long-context methods into five families (efficient attention, long-term memory, extrapolative PEs, context processing, miscellaneous) and explains RoPE's extrapolation failure by its slow dimensions never completing a period within the training length (critical dimension 92 for Llama 2 at 4k, citing Liu et al.); a taxonomy with no measured comparison of its own | [2311.12351](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12351) | ✓ [huang-2023-advancing-transformer-architecture-long-context.pdf](sources/huang-2023-advancing-transformer-architecture-long-context.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#embeddings-and-position) |

edits.old: The survey runs no comparison of its own.
edits.new: The survey reports no measured comparison of its own.
edits.why: Sec. 5 (p. 20) says 'according to Su's and our elementary experiments, ReRoPE performs very well', and the authors ship a Flash-ReRoPE kernel, so 'runs no comparison' overstates; what is true is that no numbers are reported. Taxonomy (p. 8), 92 critical dimension (p. 19) and five families verified.

doubts: v2 header says 'Manuscript submitted to ACM'; no venue found, kept as preprint.

row: | | Wang et al., *MambaByte: Token-free Selective State Space Model* (COLM 2024): a 972M byte-level Mamba trained on 150B bytes of PG-19 reached word perplexity 33.0, against 36.4 for compute-matched MEGABYTE (400B bytes) and 33.9 for a subword Mamba-1.03B on 600B; with neighbouring bytes swapped at p=0.3 its perplexity rose 28.7 points vs 630.6 for the subword model. Evaluated with a 4× longer sliding-window context; PG-19 only | [2401.13660](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.13660) | ✓ [wang-2024-mambabyte.pdf](sources/wang-2024-mambabyte.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#tokens) |
doubts: Ledger has review_status 'preprint' and no venue, but the PDF header reads 'Published as a conference paper at COLM 2024' (the note already says COLM 2024). Ledger should be updated to COLM 2024 / peer-reviewed.

row: | | Cui et al., *A Phase Transition between Positional and Semantic Learning in a Solvable Model of Dot-Product Attention* (NeurIPS 2024): for one tied, low-rank attention layer in the high-dimensional limit, the global minimum switches sharply from positional to semantic attention as samples per dimension pass a threshold, and only past it does attention beat a dense linear positional baseline. Two Gaussian tokens, identity value matrix, one head; GD was started at each minimum, and from random init Adam often found neither | [2402.03902](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03902) | ✓ [cui-2024-phase-transition-between-positional-semantic.pdf](sources/cui-2024-phase-transition-between-positional-semantic.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#embeddings-and-position) |

edits.old: From a random start, Adam reached the content-based solution less often as the dimension grew.
edits.new: From a random start, Adam at larger dimensions reached the content-based solution less often than the positional one, and often found neither.
edits.why: App. E.4 (p. 39): at d=100 Adam from uninformed init can reach either minimum; 'for larger d we observe the semantic minimum is reached less often than the positional minimum, and a considerable number of times the algorithm simply does not find either'. The paper compares semantic vs positional at larger d, not a trend in semantic hits as d grows.

doubts: Venue NeurIPS 2024 is not printed in the arXiv v2 PDF (dated 15 Oct 2024) and the paper is not in citations.db; I believe it is a NeurIPS 2024 paper but could not confirm from local sources. All other numbers (two tokens L=2, >99.8% on the counting task, identity value matrix) verified.

row: | | Lester et al., *Training LLMs over Neurally Compressed Text* (TMLR 2024): text compressed by arithmetic coding with a small LM was unlearnable at every scale from 25M to 2B (output stayed uniform); Equal-Info Windows (16-bit windows) made it learnable, reaching 0.94 bits/byte at 2B vs 0.87 for SentencePiece and 1.03 for raw bytes, with 23% fewer FLOPs/byte than SentencePiece. English C4 only; 2B models not converged | [2404.03626](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.03626) | ✓ [lester-2024-training-llms-over-neurally-compressed.pdf](sources/lester-2024-training-llms-over-neurally-compressed.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#tokens) |

| | Merrill et al., *The Illusion of State in State-Space Models* (ICML 2024): SSMs with diagonal (S4) or diagonal input-dependent (Mamba) transitions are in TC0 like transformers, so unless TC0 = NC1 they cannot compose permutations, track chess in source-target notation, or evaluate code at fixed depth; on the A5 word problem transformers, S4 and Mamba needed more layers as length grew while a one-layer RNN and the non-diagonal IDS4 did not. Worst-case bound; IDS4 not tested at LM scale | [2404.08819](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08819) | ✓ [merrill-2024-illusion-state-state-space-models.pdf](sources/merrill-2024-illusion-state-state-space-models.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#reading-a-models-size) |
doubts: Note says 'composing permutations of five elements'; the experiment uses A5 (even permutations of five elements) plus A4×Z5 and Z60. Not wrong, left as is.

row: | | Wang et al., *State Space Model for New-Generation Network Alternative to Transformers: A Survey* (Visual Intelligence 2026): collects SSM results across NLP, vision, graphs, time series and more, and from benchmarks mostly in vision (ImageNet classification, tracking, segmentation, re-ID) concludes SSMs match some transformers but stay below the state of the art, e.g. best Mamba vision backbones at 83.2% ImageNet-1K top-1, with lower memory use | [2404.09516](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.09516) | ✓ [wang-2024-state-space-model-new-generation.pdf](sources/wang-2024-state-space-model-new-generation.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#reading-a-models-size) |
doubts: Year 2026 taken from citations.db (DOI 10.1007/s44267-026-00133-1); the local PDF is arXiv v1 with a placeholder 'IEEE TRANSACTIONS' header.

row: | | Minixhofer et al., *Zero-Shot Tokenizer Transfer* (NeurIPS 2024): a hypernetwork predicts embeddings for any new tokenizer; moving Mistral-7B to 50k-token monolingual tokenizers cut sequence length 30–47% on five European languages but dropped 5-shot multilingual MMLU by 8–15 points (Russian 49.9 → 35.1) with no further training, while beating FOCUS (near chance); continued training on under 1B tokens closes much of the gap | [2405.07883](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.07883) | ✓ [minixhofer-2024-zero-shot-tokenizer-transfer.pdf](sources/minixhofer-2024-zero-shot-tokenizer-transfer.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#tokens) |

| | Muennighoff et al., *OLMoE: Open Mixture-of-Experts Language Models* (ICLR 2025): a 6.9B-total, 1.3B-active MoE (8 of 64 experts) matched a 1.3B dense model with ~3× fewer tokens but only ~2× less wall-clock (23,600 vs 37,500 tokens/s/GPU); finer experts helped (8→32 ≈ +10% on HellaSwag/MMLU, 64 only +1–2%), a shared expert slightly hurt, and upcycling from OLMo-1B was overtaken after 500B tokens. English only | [2409.02060](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.02060) | ✓ [muennighoff-2024-olmoe.pdf](sources/muennighoff-2024-olmoe.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#reading-a-models-size) |

edits.old: About 60% of routing decisions are already fixed after 1% of pretraining
edits.new: Up to about 60% of routing decisions are already fixed after 1% of pretraining
edits.why: Sec. 5.1 (p. ~19): 'after 1% of pretraining (5000 steps or 20B tokens), up to ∼60% of routing to the top-8 activated experts has already saturated' — 60% is the best layer, not the average. Everything else in the passage (3×/2×, 23,600 vs 37,500, 8→32 ≈10%, 64 +1–2%, shared expert, 54.1 vs 46.2 / 66.9 MMLU, 500B and 25% vs 120% upcycling, English only, domain specialization absent in Mixtral) verified.

doubts: ICLR 2025 from citations.db; the arXiv PDF carries no venue.

row: | | Nie et al., *Large Language Diffusion Models* (LLaDA, NeurIPS 2025): an 8B masked-diffusion model on 2.3T tokens scored 65.9 MMLU vs 65.4 for LLaMA 3 8B on 15T and 70.3 vs 48.7 on GSM8K, trailing on BBH (49.7 vs 62.1) and HellaSwag (70.5 vs 79.1); on reverse Chinese-poem completion it scored 45.6 vs GPT-4o's 34.3 (forward 51.8 vs 82.7). No KV cache, fixed generation length, compute-matched AR comparison only below 10²³ FLOPs | [2502.09992](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.09992) | ✓ [nie-2025-large-language-diffusion-models.pdf](sources/nie-2025-large-language-diffusion-models.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#reading-a-models-size) |

| | Zhu et al., *Transformers without Normalization* (DyT, CVPR 2025): replacing every norm with γ·tanh(αx)+β matched RMSNorm on LLaMA 7B–70B trained on 200B Pile tokens (loss 1.60 vs 1.59 at 7B, 1.45 for both at 70B; same zero-shot average), but needed α₀ tuned to model width, and after torch.compile the layers ran no faster than RMSNorm | [2503.10622](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.10622) | ✓ [zhu-2025-transformers-without-normalization.pdf](sources/zhu-2025-transformers-without-normalization.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#the-transformer-block-and-the-gpt-stack) |

headings.heading: The transformer block and the GPT stack

row: | | Videau et al., *From Bytes to Ideas: Language Modeling with Autoregressive U-Nets* (AU-Net, NeurIPS 2025): byte-level U-Nets pooling at spaces matched or beat a BPE transformer on the same DCLM data, e.g. 73.7 vs 70.2 HellaSwag (4-stage, 1B-width, 370B tokens); at 8B they lost on Chinese MMLU (28.0 vs 33.0) because splitting needs spaces, and on CUTE both the 7.5B BPE model (91.5%) and AU-Net (97.3%) spelled well but stayed below 25% on character edits | [2506.14761](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14761) | ✓ [videau-2025-bytes-ideas.pdf](sources/videau-2025-bytes-ideas.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#tokens) |

edits.old: cost it on Chinese MMLU (28.0 vs 33.0)
edits.new: cost it on Chinese MMLU at 8B (28.0 vs 33.0)
edits.why: The passage frames AU-Net results as 'at about 1B parameters', but the Chinese MMLU figure comes from Table 3 (right), which compares the 8B models (English 49.6 vs 51.1 matches the 8B rows of Table 2). HellaSwag 73.7 vs 70.2 is indeed the 1B-width tier (AU-Net 4 vs BPE, 370B tokens). CUTE line 130 (91.5 / 97.3, char edits <25%) verified against Table 7.

doubts: The citation appears twice in the note (lines 130 and 138, both under Tokens); one row covers both.

row: | | Hwang et al., *Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling* (H-Net, 2025 ⚑): a learned byte chunker settled near GPT-2's 4.6 bytes per chunk (4.7–4.8 for one stage), and at FLOP-matched GPT-3 XL scale (1.3B) the two-stage H-Net beat the BPE transformer on the same data, 0.715 vs 0.730 bits/byte on FineWeb-Edu and 58.2 vs 55.5 average zero-shot accuracy; nothing larger than 1.3B-equivalent was trained | [2507.07955](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07955) | ✓ [hwang-2025-dynamic-chunking-end-end-hierarchical.pdf](sources/hwang-2025-dynamic-chunking-end-end-hierarchical.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#tokens) |

edits.why: Table 2 (p. 13): 0.715 bpb / 58.2 avg is H-Net (2-stage), whose innermost chunks average 6.9 bytes (Table 1); the router 'near ~4.6 bytes per chunk' in the preceding clause is the 1-stage model (4.7 BPIC), which scored 0.728 / 56.2. Same direction, but the numbers belong to a different variant.

doubts: No venue found; kept as preprint (ledger has none).
